units.title: Starlight
units.blurb: Magnitudes and distances, dust, colors, the Planck function, and what spectral lines say about temperature.

units.title: Binary Stars and Exoplanets
units.blurb: Masses from orbits, radial-velocity curves, eclipses and transits, and planet temperatures.

units.title: How Stars Work
units.blurb: Hydrostatic equilibrium, the virial theorem, fusion and tunneling, energy transport and the limits on stellar luminosity.

units.title: Stellar Evolution and Compact Objects
units.blurb: Evolutionary tracks, degenerate matter, white dwarfs and neutron stars, black holes, tides, accretion and gravitational waves.

units.title: Galaxies and Cosmology
units.blurb: Rotation curves and dark matter, supermassive black holes, redshift and the scale factor, the Friedmann equation, the CMB and the first elements.

topics.title: Magnitude Arithmetic
topics.short: Magnitudes compare fluxes on a log scale: m₁ − m₂ = −2.5 log(F₁/F₂).
topics.trouble: Students drop the minus sign, so the brighter star gets the larger magnitude.

topics.title: Absolute Magnitude and the Distance Modulus
topics.short: A star's absolute magnitude is its magnitude seen from 10 pc, and m − M = 5 log(d/10 pc).
topics.trouble: Students put the distance in light-years, or forget the 10 pc reference.

topics.title: Interstellar Dust: Extinction and Reddening
topics.short: Dust dims and reddens starlight, adding A to the distance modulus: m − M = 5 log(d/10 pc) + A.
topics.trouble: Students take a dust-reddened star to be cooler than it is, forgetting that dust removes blue light.

topics.title: Color Index and Temperature
topics.short: The color index B − V compares two magnitudes, and a smaller value means a hotter star.
topics.trouble: Students think a larger B − V means a bluer star, when it means the star is fainter in blue light and so redder.

topics.title: The Planck Function
topics.short: B_λ(T) gives a blackbody's spectrum; its peak gives Wien's law and its area gives σT⁴.
topics.trouble: Students think a hotter blackbody is brighter only at short wavelengths, when it is brighter at every wavelength.

topics.title: Effective Temperature and Stellar Radii
topics.short: Use L = 4πR²σT_eff⁴ with real values to find the radii of dwarfs, giants and supergiants.
topics.trouble: Students forget to raise the temperature to the fourth power, or the radius to the second.

topics.title: Excitation and the Strength of Spectral Lines
topics.short: The fraction of atoms in an excited level follows (g_b/g_a)e^(−ΔE/kT), which is why hydrogen lines peak in A stars.
topics.trouble: Students think the hottest stars must show the strongest hydrogen lines.

topics.title: Ionization and the Spectral Sequence
topics.short: Rising temperature ionizes each element in turn, so the spectral classes are a temperature sequence, not a sequence of composition.
topics.trouble: Students think stars of different spectral classes are made of different elements.

topics.title: Masses from Visual Binaries
topics.short: Parallax turns angular separation into a, Kepler's third law gives M₁ + M₂, and the center of mass splits it.
topics.trouble: Students apply the third law with a in arcseconds, before converting it to AU.

topics.title: Spectroscopic Binaries
topics.short: Doppler shifts trace each star's orbit, and their speeds give the mass ratio m₁/m₂ = v₂/v₁.
topics.trouble: Students think the faster-moving star is the heavier one.

topics.title: Eclipsing Binaries
topics.short: The timing of eclipses gives the stars' radii, and the depths compare their surface temperatures.
topics.trouble: Students think the deeper eclipse happens when the bigger star is hidden, rather than the hotter one.

topics.title: Exoplanet Transits
topics.short: A transit's depth (R_p/R_*)² gives the planet's size, and its period gives the orbit.
topics.trouble: Students take the depth to be R_p/R_* instead of its square.

topics.title: Exoplanet Masses from Wobbles
topics.short: A planet's pull sets its star's velocity amplitude, which gives the planet's mass times sin i.
topics.trouble: Students think the radial-velocity method gives the planet's true mass, rather than a lower limit.

topics.title: Planet Temperatures and the Habitable Zone
topics.short: Balancing absorbed starlight against emitted heat gives T = T_*(1 − A)^(1/4)√(R_*/(2d)).
topics.trouble: Students think a planet's distance from its star alone sets its temperature, ignoring reflectivity and the star itself.

topics.title: Hydrostatic Equilibrium
topics.short: In a star, pressure balances gravity layer by layer: dP/dr = −Gm(r)ρ/r².
topics.trouble: Students think a star's gas is held up by its solid core.

topics.title: Estimating a Star's Center
topics.short: Order-of-magnitude estimates give P_c ~ GM²/R⁴ and T_c ~ GMm_p/(kR), millions of kelvins for the Sun.
topics.trouble: Students think the Sun's center is about as hot as its surface.

topics.title: The Virial Theorem
topics.short: For a gas ball held by its own gravity, 2K + U = 0, so losing energy makes it contract and heat up.
topics.trouble: Students think a star that radiates energy must cool down.

topics.title: Gravity as a Power Source
topics.short: Contraction alone could power the Sun for only the Kelvin–Helmholtz time GM²/(RL), about 30 million years.
topics.trouble: Students think the Sun could shine for billions of years by shrinking alone.

topics.title: The Proton–Proton Chain and the CNO Cycle
topics.short: Four protons become helium-4 and release 26.7 MeV; the CNO cycle takes over in hotter, heavier stars.
topics.trouble: Students think stars fuse four protons at once in a single collision.

topics.title: Why Fusion Needs Tunneling
topics.short: The Coulomb barrier is far higher than kT in the Sun's core, so protons fuse only by tunneling.
topics.trouble: Students think the Sun's core is hot enough for protons to climb over the Coulomb barrier.

topics.title: Radiation and Convection Inside Stars
topics.short: Photons random-walk outward, so N steps of length ℓ cover only √N·ℓ, and the trip out of the Sun takes on the order of 100,000 years.
topics.trouble: Students think light made in the core reaches the surface in a few seconds.

topics.title: The Mass–Luminosity Relation
topics.short: On the main sequence L ∝ M^3.5 roughly, so lifetimes go as M^(−2.5).
topics.trouble: Students think a star twice as massive is twice as luminous.

topics.title: The Eddington Luminosity
topics.short: Radiation pressure on electrons balances gravity at L_Edd ≈ 3.3 × 10⁴ (M/M_⊙) L_⊙.
topics.trouble: Students think a star can be as luminous as it likes, whatever its mass.

topics.title: Solar Neutrinos
topics.short: Neutrinos leave the core at once, letting us see fusion directly, and their changing flavors solved the solar neutrino problem.
topics.trouble: Students think neutrinos are blocked by the Sun's layers, like light.

topics.title: Evolutionary Tracks
topics.short: A star's path across the H–R diagram follows the changes in its core.
topics.trouble: Students think stars move along the main sequence as they age.

topics.title: Electron Degeneracy Pressure
topics.short: The exclusion principle makes packed electrons push back even when they are cold.
topics.trouble: Students think a white dwarf is held up by hot gas pressure.

topics.title: The White Dwarf Mass–Radius Relation
topics.short: Degeneracy gives R ∝ M^(−1/3), so heavier white dwarfs are smaller.
topics.trouble: Students think more massive white dwarfs must be bigger.

topics.title: The Chandrasekhar Limit
topics.short: Electrons moving near light speed can hold up at most about 1.4 solar masses.
topics.trouble: Students think the limit applies to the whole star rather than to its core or remnant.

topics.title: Core-Collapse Supernovae
topics.short: An iron core collapses in under a second, and neutrinos carry off about 10⁴⁶ J.
topics.trouble: Students think most of a supernova's energy leaves as light.

topics.title: Neutron Stars
topics.short: A collapsing core keeps its angular momentum and magnetic flux, so neutron stars spin fast with huge fields.
topics.trouble: Students think a neutron star spins slowly because the original star did.

topics.title: Pulsar Spin-Down
topics.short: A pulsar's lost rotational energy, dE/dt = Iωω̇, powers the nebula around it.
topics.trouble: Students think a pulsar shines because it is still hot from the explosion, rather than by spending its spin.

topics.title: The Schwarzschild Radius
topics.short: r_s = 2GM/c², about 3 km for each solar mass.
topics.trouble: Students think a black hole's pull at a given distance is stronger than the star's that formed it.

topics.title: Gravitational Redshift and Time Dilation
topics.short: A clock at radius r runs slow by √(1 − r_s/r) compared with one far away.
topics.trouble: Students mix up gravitational time dilation with the time dilation of motion.

topics.title: Tidal Forces and the Roche Limit
topics.short: The difference in gravity across a body, about 2GMmΔr/r³, tears apart moons and stretches matter near black holes.
topics.trouble: Students think tidal force falls off as 1/r², like gravity itself, rather than 1/r³.

topics.title: Accretion Power
topics.short: Matter falling onto a compact object releases about GMṁ/R, far more per kilogram than fusion near a neutron star.
topics.trouble: Students think fusion always releases more energy per kilogram than falling.

topics.title: Gravitational Waves
topics.short: Orbiting compact objects radiate gravitational waves and spiral inward; LIGO first detected merging black holes in 2015.
topics.trouble: Students think gravitational waves are sound waves in space, or the same as gravity waves in water and air.

topics.title: Rotation Curves and Dark Matter
topics.short: v(r) = √(GM(r)/r), so a flat rotation curve needs mass that grows in proportion to r.
topics.trouble: Students miss why a flat curve is a surprise: the visible mass alone predicts that outer stars should orbit more slowly.

topics.title: Supermassive Black Holes
topics.short: Stars orbiting the center of the Milky Way weigh its black hole at about 4 million suns.
topics.trouble: Students think the central black hole holds most of the galaxy's mass.

topics.title: The Cosmic Distance Ladder
topics.short: Parallax calibrates Cepheids, Cepheids calibrate type Ia supernovae, and each rung reaches farther.
topics.trouble: Students think one method measures distances all the way out.

topics.title: Redshift and the Scale Factor
topics.short: 1 + z = λ_observed/λ_emitted = a(now)/a(then): light stretches as space expands.
topics.trouble: Students think a cosmological redshift is only a Doppler shift from galaxies moving through space.

topics.title: Hubble's Law in Practice
topics.short: For small z, d ≈ cz/H₀, and 1/H₀ sets the age scale of the universe.
topics.trouble: Students use d = cz/H₀ for large z, where it fails.

topics.title: The Friedmann Equation and Critical Density
topics.short: H² = 8πGρ/3 − kc²/a², so a flat universe has the critical density 3H²/(8πG).
topics.trouble: Students think "flat universe" means a universe shaped like a pancake.

topics.title: Matter, Radiation and Dark Energy Through Time
topics.short: Matter thins as a⁻³, radiation as a⁻⁴, and dark energy stays constant, so each ruled in turn.
topics.trouble: Students think the mix of matter and radiation in the universe has always been the same.

topics.title: The Cosmic Microwave Background
topics.short: The background's temperature scales as 1/a: 2.725 K today, about 3000 K when atoms formed.
topics.trouble: Students think the microwave background comes from one place in the sky, where the Big Bang happened.

topics.title: Big Bang Nucleosynthesis
topics.short: In its first minutes the universe made about 25% helium by mass, matching what we measure.
topics.trouble: Students think all of the helium in the universe was made in stars.
